column5: The word near at mouth and heart
column6: The commentary says the feminine “it” is the reminder offered in 87:9 and that the worst person keeps it beside him yet at a remove; Deuteronomy says the command is not far away but very near, in mouth and heart, to be done.

column5: “Depart from us” and rejected knowledge
column6: The commentary makes the ashqa actively turn away from the reminder; Job quotes the wicked saying to God to depart and that they do not desire knowledge of his ways, a direct speech of refusal, while Job’s context complicates any claim that such rejection is always punished immediately.

column5: Wisdom calls and is refused
column6: The commentary says the same reminder is offered and the difference begins in the hearer; Wisdom says she called and was refused, making rejection rather than the offer the decisive act.

column5: Counsel and reproof rejected
column6: The commentary’s “most wretched” turns aside from admonition; Wisdom says her counsel was rejected and her reproof ignored, then describes the consequence of that response.

column5: Turning the ear from Torah
column6: The commentary treats turning from reminder as choosing wrongly what to keep at one’s side; Proverbs says the person who turns an ear away from hearing Torah makes even prayer abhorrent.

column5: Not listening and walking backward
column6: The commentary distinguishes the unchanged reminder from the hearer’s response; Jeremiah says the people did not listen or incline their ear, but followed their own counsel and went backward.

column5: Stopping the ear against prophetic words
column6: The commentary’s ashqa keeps the reminder at hand but declines it; Zechariah says the people refused to hear, turned a stubborn shoulder, and stopped their ears against the law and the words sent through prophets.

column5: A hardened heart and unanswered warning
column6: The commentary connects rejection of the reminder with the person’s own chosen posture; Zechariah says they made their hearts hard so they would not hear the law or prophetic words, followed by the Lord’s anger.

column5: Hearing without doing
column6: The commentary says the reminder itself is unchanged while people respond differently; Ezekiel’s hearers come, sit before the prophet, and hear his words, but do not do them because their hearts pursue gain.

column5: The prophet as a pleasing song
column6: The commentary’s image of keeping admonition nearby yet treating it as alien fits Ezekiel’s hearers, who enjoy the prophet’s voice like a lovely song while not carrying out what he says.

column5: “Today” as an open moment to hear
column6: The commentary presents one reminder offered to all, with the response still open; the psalm addresses its hearers as God’s people and says that today they hear his voice.

column5: Do not harden the heart
column6: The commentary contrasts the one who takes warning with the one who avoids it; the psalm warns its hearers not to harden their hearts as in the wilderness rebellion.

column5: The Rechabites obey while Judah will not hear
column6: The commentary says the same reminder reaches different hearers; Jeremiah contrasts Rechabites who kept their father’s command with Judah, which did not listen when God spoke persistently through prophets.

column5: A messenger must speak whether hearers heed or refuse
column6: The commentary separates the act of offering reminder from its reception; Ezekiel is told that the rebellious may hear or refuse, but will know a prophet has been among them.

column5: Responsibility after a warning is given
column6: The commentary says the messenger offers admonition without controlling the hearer; Ezekiel’s watchman is delivered from guilt after warning, while the warned wicked person remains accountable if he does not turn.

column5: Repeated messengers sent in compassion
column6: The commentary emphasizes a single shared call and differing reception; Chronicles says God repeatedly sent messengers because he had compassion on his people and dwelling place.

column5: Mocking and despising the words
column6: The commentary’s worst person avoids the reminder and faces its consequence; Chronicles says the people mocked God’s messengers, despised his words, and scoffed at the prophets until judgment came.

column5: Rejecting knowledge and forgetting Torah
column6: The commentary links the wretched condition to turning away from reminder; Hosea names the people’s rejection of knowledge and forgetting of God’s law as the cause of their ruin.

column5: Nineveh receives the warning
column6: The commentary says the offered reminder is the same while its hearers divide by response; in Jonah, the people of Nineveh believe the warning and undertake repentance rather than dismiss it.

column5: Turning from evil changes the outcome
column6: The commentary contrasts turning away from reminder with self-correction; Jonah says God saw that Nineveh turned from its evil way and relented from the announced disaster.

column5: Human choice and self-directed action
column6: The commentary reads the response verbs as acts a person does upon oneself; Sirach says God left human beings in the hand of their own inclination, giving a Jewish wisdom parallel for accountable response.

column5: Fire and water set before the hearer
column6: The commentary says the same reminder is offered but people choose their response; Sirach pictures fire and water before the person, who stretches out a hand to whichever he chooses.

column5: Life and death as alternatives
column6: The commentary places the wretched person at the far end of a chosen response; Sirach explicitly sets life and death before human beings and says each receives what he chooses.

column5: Abraham’s family served other gods
column6: The commentary recalls Abraham asking God to keep him and his sons from idol worship; Joshua says Abraham’s ancestors, including Terah, served other gods, supplying the biblical background to the Qur’anic break with idolatry.

column5: The word received and made fruitful
column6: The commentary contrasts one who takes reminder with the one who avoids it; Mark’s good soil hears the word, accepts it, and bears fruit, a concrete positive reception.

column5: Hearing and doing as the wise response
column6: The commentary reads taking reminder and purifying oneself as actions a person undertakes; Jesus calls the hearer who does his words wise and compares him to a house built on rock.

column5: Hearing without doing as the ruinous response
column6: The commentary’s ashqa hears the reminder’s availability yet turns aside; Jesus describes the hearer who does not do his words, whose house falls when the same storm comes.

column5: Moses and the Prophets are already available
column6: The commentary says the reminder has been delivered and the hearer is responsible for receiving it; Abraham in the parable tells the rich man’s brothers that they have Moses and the Prophets to hear.

column5: A further sign will not cure refusal to hear
column6: The commentary says those avoiding reminder cannot blame its absence; the parable answers that those who do not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead.

column5: Felix fears, then sends Paul away
column6: The commentary contrasts the one who fears and receives warning with the worst person who turns from it; as Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control, and coming judgment, Felix becomes afraid and tells him to go away.

column5: Resisting the Spirit as the ancestors did
column6: The commentary portrays turning away from reminder as a repeated response to divine messengers; Stephen accuses his hearers of resisting the Holy Spirit and doing as their ancestors did when they rejected the prophets.

column5: Turning away from the living God
column6: The commentary’s verb makes withdrawal the person’s own act; Hebrews warns against an unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.

column5: Do not harden the heart when the voice is heard
column6: The commentary links the reminder to a present chance to respond; Hebrews repeats the psalm’s “Today” warning not to harden the heart upon hearing God’s voice.

column5: The message heard but not beneficial
column6: The commentary says one unchanged reminder benefits one hearer while another avoids it; Hebrews says the good news came to its hearers but did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith.

column5: One proclamation among both saved and perishing
column6: The commentary stresses one reminder offered to all with different reception; Paul calls the apostolic proclamation an aroma of Christ among both those being saved and those perishing.

column5: The same word as life or death
column6: The commentary says the same reminder yields benefit to one and loss to another; Paul describes the proclamation as an aroma from death to death for one group and from life to life for another.

column5: The word of the cross divides hearers
column6: The commentary says the reminder itself is unchanged while people receive it differently; Paul says the word of the cross is foolishness to those perishing and God’s power to those being saved.

column5: Doers, not hearers only
column6: The commentary emphasizes that the person does something to himself by taking or avoiding reminder; James tells hearers to become doers of the word and not deceive themselves by hearing alone.

column5: The hearer who sees and forgets
column6: The commentary contrasts the Prophet’s preserved recitation with the person who lets reminder pass; James likens the hearer who does not act to someone who looks at his face in a mirror.

column5: The hearer turns away and forgets
column6: The commentary’s image is of one who moves the reminder aside; James says the inactive hearer goes away and immediately forgets what he was like.

column5: Persevering in the word and doing it
column6: The commentary links self-directed purification to sustained action; James contrasts the forgetful hearer with the one who looks into the law, perseveres, and acts.

column5: One sermon meets mockery and postponement
column6: The commentary says the reminder is offered but response divides hearers; after Paul speaks of resurrection, some mock and others postpone hearing him again.

column5: Some hearers join and believe
column6: The commentary contrasts the worst person with one who takes the reminder; Acts adds that some listeners join Paul and believe after the same speech that others mocked.

column5: Not all obey the good news they hear
column6: The commentary makes reception rather than delivery the point of division; Paul says not all obeyed the good news and cites the question of who believed the report.

column5: Jesus’ words are offered for salvation
column6: The commentary says the reminder is given for benefit, even though its hearers may turn away; Jesus says he came to save the world rather than judge the one who hears his words.

column5: The rejected word judges its hearer
column6: The commentary connects avoiding reminder with the coming fire and consequence; Jesus says the one who rejects him and does not receive his words has a judge, and the word will judge him on the last day.

column5: Seeking death but unable to die
column6: The commentary reads the condemned state as neither dying nor living; Revelation says those tormented in the vision seek death but cannot find it, a striking parallel with the refusal of death as release.

column5: Abraham taken from beyond the River
column6: The commentary says Abraham asks God to keep him away from idols rather than trusting his own power; Joshua recalls God taking Abraham from beyond the River and leading him, a related account of Abraham’s separation under divine guidance.

column5: Pharaoh refuses Moses’ demand
column6: The commentary describes Moses inviting Pharaoh to purify himself and then Pharaoh denying and turning away; Exodus has Pharaoh answer Moses and Aaron by asking who the Lord is and refusing to obey his voice, a shared confrontation whose wording and demand differ.

column5: Two outcomes placed before Israel
column6: The commentary develops the division between the one who remembers and the one who avoids reminder; Deuteronomy sets life and good against death and evil before Israel as a covenant decision.

column5: “Choose life” after the warning
column6: The commentary says the response, not the offered reminder, divides people; Moses calls heaven and earth to witness and urges Israel to choose life, making the decision explicit.

column5: Wisdom speaks publicly in the streets
column6: The commentary says the reminder is not delivered privately to only one favored hearer; Proverbs portrays Wisdom crying aloud in public places, where the invitation can be heard before some reject it.

column5: Eating the fruit of one’s own way
column6: The commentary describes the response as what a person does to himself by moving the reminder aside; Wisdom says the refusers will eat the fruit of their own way, making consequence follow chosen conduct.

column5: Safety for the one who listens
column6: The commentary contrasts the ashqa with the one who takes reminder; Wisdom promises that the one who listens will dwell securely, giving the positive outcome beside the warning of refusal.

column5: A people unwilling to hear instruction
column6: The commentary describes people who choose to turn from reminder; Isaiah calls the people rebellious children unwilling to hear the Lord’s instruction.

column5: Requesting smooth words instead of warning
column6: The commentary says the wretched person treats beneficial reminder as something to avoid; Isaiah’s hearers tell seers not to see and ask for smooth, agreeable things rather than truth.

column5: Prophets sent repeatedly, but no listening
column6: The commentary distinguishes the universal offer from the hearer’s response; Jeremiah says the Lord persistently sent prophets, yet the people did not listen or incline their ear.

column5: A call to turn from evil is ignored
column6: The commentary links rejecting reminder with refusing the offered chance to change; Jeremiah recounts repeated calls to turn from evil and serve God, which Judah did not heed.

column5: Neighbors invite one another to hear the prophet
column6: The commentary’s side image says the reminder is beside the person, not far away; Ezekiel describes people speaking to one another and inviting one another to hear the Lord’s word from the prophet.

column5: Seek the Lord while near
column6: The commentary says the rejected reminder has reached the hearer and remains within reach; Isaiah urges seeking the Lord while he may be found and calling while he is near.

column5: Turning back is still invited
column6: The commentary contrasts the person who takes the reminder with the person who avoids it; Isaiah calls the wicked to forsake his way and return to the Lord for mercy.

column5: The resident alien is to be loved as oneself
column6: The commentary develops “foreign neighbor” as an image for someone kept beside but treated as unrelated; Leviticus commands Israel to love the resident alien as oneself, an ethical counterpoint to treating the nearby reminder as foreign.

column5: A famine of hearing the Lord’s words
column6: The commentary stresses that the reminder is offered now and can be put aside; Amos announces a later famine of hearing the Lord’s words, a reversal in which people will lack what the commentary’s hearers still have.

column5: Searching for a word that cannot be found
column6: The commentary says the wretched person lets a present reminder pass by; Amos portrays people wandering in search of the Lord’s word and not finding it, sharpening the cost of refusing it while available.

column5: Unquenched fire and undying worm
column6: The commentary connects the worst person’s refusal with the great fire and the condition of neither dying nor living; Isaiah pictures the corpses of rebels under an unquenched fire and undying worm, sharing persistent judgment imagery but describing corpses rather than the same paradox of living punishment.

column5: The wicked later see the righteous vindicated
column6: The commentary says the one who avoids reminder discovers too late what he has lost; Wisdom depicts the wicked seeing the righteous honored and confessing that they once misjudged him.

column5: A belated confession of straying from truth
column6: The commentary connects refusal of reminder to a path whose loss becomes clear after judgment; Wisdom’s wicked confess that they strayed from the way of truth and did not know the path of righteousness.

column5: Two spirits and two paths to opposed outcomes
column6: The commentary develops a person’s response as the dividing choice between outcomes; the Community Rule organizes human conduct under spirits and paths of truth/light or perversity/darkness, giving a Second Temple Jewish version of moral division.

column5: The seed is the word
column6: The commentary says the one reminder is offered while reception differs; Jesus identifies the seed as the word, so the parable makes the hearer’s response determine whether the same sowing bears fruit.

column5: Initial reception can fail under pressure
column6: The commentary’s “remembering” is not merely hearing once; Mark describes hearers who receive the word with joy but fall away when tribulation or persecution comes.

column5: Worldly cares choke the word
column6: The commentary connects rejection of reminder to preferring worldly life; Mark says cares, wealth’s deceit, and other desires enter and choke the word so it becomes fruitless.

column5: Hearing without understanding or turning
column6: The commentary distinguishes a person who receives reminder from one who turns away; Jesus cites Isaiah about people who hear without understanding and have closed their eyes lest they turn and be healed.

column5: Jerusalem was unwilling to be gathered
column6: The commentary says the reminder can be offered while its audience chooses distance; Jesus laments that he wanted to gather Jerusalem’s children but they were unwilling.

column5: Take care how you hear
column6: The commentary says response to the reminder, not its delivery, distinguishes hearers; Jesus warns listeners to take care how they hear, since what one has can be taken away or increased.

column5: The rich man turns away from a life-giving invitation
column6: The commentary connects avoidance of reminder with preferring worldly life; Mark says the man who was invited to sell his possessions and follow Jesus went away grieving because he had great wealth.

column5: Cleanse yourselves and draw near
column6: The commentary reads purification as work a person does upon himself; James calls double-minded people to cleanse their hands, purify their hearts, and draw near to God.

column5: The hopeful person purifies himself
column6: The commentary groups remembering, avoiding, and purifying as self-directed actions; John says the one who hopes in Christ purifies himself as Christ is pure.

column5: The warning remains “Today”
column6: The commentary treats reminder as presently available and response as decisive; Hebrews says God again appoints a day called Today and repeats the warning not to harden the heart.

column5: No rest from the torment
column6: The commentary’s condemned person neither dies nor lives and endures prolonged hardship; Revelation says the worshippers of the beast have no rest day or night, a related but differently framed image of unending punishment.

column5: Welcoming the stranger
column6: The commentary develops the nearby reminder as treated like a foreign neighbor; Jesus identifies himself with the stranger who is welcomed, making reception of the socially distant one a test of response.

column5: The unquenched fire
column6: The commentary connects the worst person with the great fire and an unending state; Jesus invokes Gehenna where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched, sharing persistence imagery without equating the scenes.

column5: Two ways, life and death
column6: The commentary develops a sharp division between the one who takes reminder and the one who avoids it; the Didache opens by setting out a way of life and a way of death and stressing the great difference between them.

column5: The way of death
column6: The commentary names a worst person by the path he chooses; the Didache’s catalogue of the way of death includes people who hate truth and love falsehood, giving an early Christian moral portrait of that path.

column5: Way of light and way of darkness
column6: The commentary’s paired outcomes turn on a person’s response; Barnabas opens its “Two Ways” teaching with the way of light and the way of darkness, adding an early Christian moral framework for opposed paths.

column5: The word accomplishes its purpose
column6: The commentary emphasizes a reminder whose hearers may take it or turn away; Isaiah says the word sent by God will accomplish what he desires, a different emphasis on the efficacy of the divine word rather than a claim that every hearer responds alike.
